Two benefits plans do not turn one bill into two reimbursements: chart the coordination

Split a hypothetical invoice between two plans and the household, compare standalone amounts with coordinated payments and stress unused maximums in four charts.

By TickerLantern Research · Published 25 October 2026 · 6 min read
Sources reviewed 25 October 2026

Change an assumption. Follow the result.

Coordinate two hypothetical plan amounts against one common eligible expense

Interactive planning lab

Primary payment under the selected teaching formula$1,000
Coordinated secondary payment under that formula$500
Household share, including the separately ineligible amount$200

Original two-plan teaching formula, not an insurer claim decision. Primary and secondary status are assumed already confirmed; this calculator does not determine or let the claimant choose priority. Both plans are assumed to use the same entered eligible expense. Primary pays the lesser of its percentage amount and unused maximum. Secondary pays the least of the remaining common eligible expense, its standalone percentage amount and its unused maximum. The secondary percentage applies to the original common eligible expense, not to the unpaid remainder. The separately entered ineligible amount is covered by neither plan. No deductible, differing eligible-fee schedules, exclusions, service limits, tax, premium, claim date or reimbursement delay is modeled. Rates, maximums and eligibility must be checked in the actual plans; different terms require different calculations.

The central idea

The eligible expense, the order of payment, each plan’s remaining maximum and the coordination calculation all matter. Two headline percentages cannot simply be added to predict cash received.

01

Establish the eligible expense and the plan order first

Coverage under two health or dental plans does not mean the household can collect each plan’s headline percentage independently. The plans coordinate payments for the expense, and the actual outcome depends on the applicable terms.

Canada Life’s coordination overview describes a primary payer, a secondary payer and submitting the first plan’s benefit statement with the remaining claim. Its examples also show that priority depends on the coverage circumstances. The calculator assumes the order has already been confirmed.

The model does not choose which plan should pay first, check dependent eligibility or decide that a service qualifies. It begins with a common amount assumed eligible on the same basis under both plans. Actual plans can recognize different eligible amounts and require a different calculation.

02

A fully reimbursed eligible amount may still leave part of the invoice

The example has CAD 1,500 assumed eligible under both plans and a separate CAD 200 invoiced amount assumed ineligible under both. The total bill is therefore CAD 1,700. Entering these separately prevents the entire provider charge being mistaken for an automatically covered expense.

CLHIA’s consumer explanation notes that combined reimbursement cannot exceed the eligible expense and can be lower than the amount charged. A plan’s recognized fees and limits can matter even when another plan has already made a payment.

The model’s CAD 200 is not a deductible or an estimate of a typical fee difference. It is an independent amount outside both plans’ assumed eligibility. Any actual difference between a provider’s invoice and each plan’s recognized expense needs confirmation from the benefit statements and plan documents.

03

Write the secondary formula instead of assuming it

In this teaching contract, the primary payment is the lesser of its percentage of the common eligible expense and its unused maximum available for the claim. The secondary standalone amount is calculated the same way using its own percentage and maximum.

The coordinated secondary payment is then the least of three amounts: the unpaid part of the common eligible expense, the secondary standalone percentage amount and the secondary unused maximum. Its percentage applies to the original common eligible amount, rather than to the unpaid remainder.

That is an explicit model convention. An actual plan may have different eligible fees, deductibles, limits or secondary-payment terms. The public source establishes the need for coordination; it does not certify these entered percentages, maximums or the result for a real claim.

04

Follow one CAD 1,500 eligible expense through both calculations

The primary rate is 70%. Applied to CAD 1,500, it produces CAD 1,050 before the unused maximum. The selected primary maximum is CAD 1,000, so the modeled primary payment is CAD 1,000. CAD 500 of the common eligible expense remains unpaid.

The secondary rate is 60%, giving a standalone percentage amount of CAD 900. Its unused maximum is CAD 1,000. Coordination limits the secondary payment to the remaining CAD 500, so it pays CAD 500 under the stated formula.

The two payments total CAD 1,500. They fully reimburse the common eligible amount in this example while leaving the CAD 200 separately ineligible amount to the household. The first stacked bar therefore reconciles CAD 1,000 + CAD 500 + CAD 200 = CAD 1,700.

05

Seventy percent plus sixty percent is not a 130% payment

The second chart compares each plan’s modeled standalone amount with its coordinated payment. The primary’s CAD 1,000 amount stays unchanged. The secondary’s CAD 900 standalone amount becomes CAD 500 after applying the unpaid-expense ceiling.

Adding the two standalone amounts would give CAD 1,900. That exceeds the common eligible expense by CAD 400. It describes an uncoordinated sum that the model does not pay, rather than extra money available to the household.

The unused maximum is also different from a reimbursement percentage. A CAD 1,000 maximum does not mean that CAD 1,000 will be paid on any claim. The percentage calculation and the eligible amount can produce a smaller benefit before coordination is even considered.

06

Use what remains available, rather than an original annual headline

Reduce the secondary unused maximum from CAD 1,000 to CAD 200. Its potential standalone amount is now limited to CAD 200, and its coordinated payment is also CAD 200. The primary still pays CAD 1,000.

The household then funds CAD 300 of the common eligible expense plus the separate CAD 200, for CAD 500 in total. A second plan exists, but that fact alone does not complete the reimbursement.

The controls accept unused amounts available for this claim. They do not reconstruct earlier claims, reset benefits at a calendar anniversary or determine whether several services share one maximum. Verify the relevant benefit category and period before entering an amount from a coverage summary.

07

Read the claim-size curve as separate scenarios

The line chart increases the common eligible expense while holding rates, unused maximums and the separately ineligible amount fixed. It compares the household share with only the primary plan against the share with both modeled plans.

At smaller claim sizes, the percentages can determine the result. At larger sizes, the selected maximums can limit both payments, leaving a growing amount for the household. With the default CAD 1,000 maximum available under each plan, combined payments cannot exceed CAD 2,000 even when the common eligible expense becomes much larger.

These points are alternative claim sizes. They are not successive claims consuming an annual balance, observations of medical prices or predictions of what treatment will cost. The ineligible CAD 200 remains a fixed additional amount in every scenario.

08

The final household share and the upfront cash need are different questions

The matrix replaces the primary and secondary unused maximums. It leaves both rates and both expense inputs selected. Each cell reports the household share under the same teaching formula, including the amount ineligible under both plans.

A small final household share does not prove that only that much cash is needed on the invoice date. If the household must first pay the full CAD 1,700 and reimbursements arrive later, it needs funding for that interval. Direct billing, assignment and claim processing need separate confirmation. The reimbursement-timing article covers that calendar.

  1. Confirm who is covered and which plan pays first.
  2. Read the eligible amount and first payer’s benefit statement.
  3. Check the secondary plan’s actual formula and unused limits.
  4. Keep any ineligible charges in the household budget.
  5. Match invoice and reimbursement dates before relying on the eventual payments.

Neither the existence of two plans nor a combined percentage establishes complete coverage. A clear calculation and a dated cash plan make the remaining commitment visible.

Sources and scope

Public sources reviewed on 25 October 2026. All four charts use an original two-plan teaching formula with a common eligible-expense basis. They contain no actual claimant, policy, provider quote, benefit entitlement or medical recommendation. Recheck current issuer documents for any product-specific decision.
